questions.prompt: A backed-up Azure VM has been deleted. You want to recover it from a valid point. Which mode fits this situation?

options.text: Create new VM, or restore disks and construct a VM.
options.explanation: These modes do not require the original VM resource to exist.

options.text: Replace existing disks on the deleted VM.
options.explanation: Replace existing requires an existing target VM.
A schedule does not recreate the deleted resource.
Alert response state does not restore the VM.

questions.prompt: A recovery point is crash-consistent. What should you expect during recovery?

options.text: Every in-memory write is guaranteed present.
options.explanation: Crash consistency captures on-disk state, not all pending memory writes.

options.text: Application/OS recovery may be needed for the captured disk state.
options.explanation: Crash-consistent recovery can require checks or transaction recovery.

options.text: The point cannot contain any disk data.
It is automatically a database transaction-log backup.
options.explanation: VM consistency is not equivalent to database log backup.

questions.prompt: Azure reports a VM restore job completed. Which two checks establish practical recovery better than the job state alone?

options.text: Verify the restored VM boots with its intended disks/network.
options.explanation: Infrastructure usability needs a direct check.

options.text: Assume every external DNS entry changed automatically.
options.explanation: External references may need independent repair.

options.text: Verify guest data and application behavior at the restored point.
options.explanation: Business recovery requires more than resource creation.

options.text: Delete the recovery points immediately before checking the app.
options.explanation: That removes fallback without establishing usability.
